hints: Look carefully at where the dark chromosomes are in each of the four photos, scattered, pulled apart, at the poles, or in two new nuclei.
Remember metaphase has one very distinctive pattern, all chromosomes lined up in a single neat row on the equator, and ask if you can see that pattern anywhere.
walkthrough:
**Recall what each stage looks like**

Think of mitosis as a story of chromosomes. In prophase they condense and become visible, in metaphase they line up in the middle, in anaphase sister chromatids separate to opposite poles, and in telophase two new nuclei reform.

**Match each photo to a stage**

Top left shows long, tangled, condensing chromosomes filling the nucleus, that is prophase. Bottom right shows V-shaped chromatids moving apart toward opposite poles, that is anaphase. Top right shows chromosome groups arrived at the poles, and bottom left shows two separate daughter cells with reforming nuclei, both are telophase and cytokinesis stages.

**Spot the missing stage**

None of the photos shows chromosomes all aligned in one straight line across the cell equator. That equatorial plate is the hallmark of metaphase, so metaphase is not shown.

options.A: Anaphase is shown in the bottom right photo where sister chromatids are clearly separating toward opposite poles.
options.B: Prophase is shown in the top left photo where chromosomes have condensed and are visible as dark tangled threads.
options.C: Metaphase is not shown because no photo shows chromosomes lined up in a single row on the metaphase plate at the equator.
options.D: Telophase is shown in the top right and bottom left photos where chromosomes are at the poles and two new nuclei are reforming.
